edges.effect_quant: In a 602-person multiethnic cohort, poorer sleep efficiency was associated with higher insulin resistance at the upper risk tail (quantile estimate 0.20, 95% CI 0.04 to 0.36). In 829 adolescents, higher actigraphy-derived sleep efficiency tracked a lower composite metabolic-risk score and more favorable waist circumference, blood pressure, HDL, and fat-mass profiles. Even in a small but very active older cohort, lower sleep efficiency was associated with a worse metabolic syndrome risk score in men.
edges.population: children, adolescents, and older adults undergoing objective sleep measurement and cardiometabolic risk phenotyping
edges.mechanism: Low sleep efficiency usually means more fragmented and less restorative sleep. That fragmentation can amplify sympathetic tone, worsen next-day glucose handling, and disrupt blood pressure and lipid regulation, making cardiometabolic control less stable over time.
edges.summary: The safest claim is that low objective sleep efficiency is a harmful cardiometabolic signal rather than a benign sleep quirk. The evidence is not yet trial-grade, but across actigraphy and polysomnography cohorts, people who spend less of the night actually asleep tend to show worse insulin resistance or broader metabolic-risk profiles.
edges.caveats: Most evidence is observational and uses mixed cardiometabolic composites rather than hard event outcomes such as myocardial infarction. Associations also vary by age, sex, and background risk, so this edge should be read as a risk-marker relationship, not proof that improving sleep efficiency alone will automatically reverse cardiometabolic disease.
